The philosophical school of phenomenology, founded by Edmund Husserl, represents a radical shift from empirical science. It is not concerned with the 'what' of an object (its physical properties, its causal relations) but the 'how' of its appearance in our consciousness. The phenomenological method demands a "bracketing" of the "natural attitude"—that is, we must suspend our ingrained belief in the objective reality of the world independent of our experience of it. This suspension, or epoché, is not a denial of the world's existence but a methodological tool to access the "things themselves" as they are given to consciousness. This "givenness" is what Husserl terms the "phenomenon." A phenomenon is not a mere mental image; it is the correlate of the intentional act of consciousness. Consciousness, in this view, is always "consciousness of something"; it is inherently directed towards an object. This "intentionality" is the foundational structure of all experience. Therefore, to understand a "tree," the phenomenologist does not study its botanical classification or its molecular structure. Instead, they meticulously describe the experience of perceiving the tree: the play of light on its leaves, the texture of its bark as felt, the sense of its "treeness" as it constitutes itself in the perceptual act. This descriptive science of "pure essences" aims to uncover the fundamental structures of consciousness that make any experience, including scientific inquiry itself, possible. Q- What is the primary purpose of the phenomenological epoché?

questions.question: Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow. The dialectic between the signifier and the signified is at the heart of semiotics. Ferdinand de Saussure, a progenitor of modern linguistics, posited that the relationship between a linguistic sign (the signifier, or the sound/image) and its conceptual meaning (the signified) is fundamentally arbitrary. There is no inherent, natural reason why the collection of sounds "d-o-g" refers to a canine mammal. This arbitrariness, however, does not imply a lack of structure; rather, the meaning is derived differentially. A word gains its meaning not from a positive, intrinsic value, but from its opposition to all other words in the linguistic system. This "diacritical" nature of language means that 'dog' is 'dog' precisely because it is not 'cat,' 'log,' or 'fog.' This entire system of arbitrary and differential signs is what constitutes a language, a social contract that interlocutors tacitly accept. To challenge this is to challenge the very foundation of codified communication. Q- What is the central thesis of the passage?

His works are often dismissed as mere Gothic sensationalism, exercises in the macabre for its own sake. This is a profound misreading.
